lessons.title: Semantic HTML: landmarks, headings and real controls
lessons.summary: How markup becomes the accessibility tree, why native elements carry behaviour that ARIA cannot add, and how to structure a page with landmarks and headings.
lessons.body: ## The core idea HTML is not a styling language. Every element carries a **meaning** (a role, a name, a state) that the browser exposes to the **accessibility tree**, to search engines, to reader mode, to password managers and to browser extensions. Semantic HTML means picking the element that matches what the content *is*, so all of those consumers get the right information without extra code. The payoff is concrete. A real `
keyPoints: Browsers expose every element as role, name and state in the accessibility tree; assistive tech reads that tree, not your CSS.
Native controls carry behaviour: a button is focusable, fires on Enter and Space, can be disabled and submits forms. ARIA adds none of that.
Landmarks (header, nav, main, aside, footer) and a ranked h1 to h6 outline are how screen-reader users navigate a page.
The HTML5 outline algorithm was never implemented and was removed from the spec; heading levels are what you write.
Use dialog, details/summary and the popover attribute before building custom overlays and disclosures.
interview: How do landmarks and the heading outline help screen-reader users, and how would you structure a typical page?
Why should a clickable control be a button rather than a div with a click handler?

check.q: You add role="button" to a div with a click handler. What does the role give you?
options: Keyboard focus and Enter/Space activation
Only the announced role; focus and keyboard handling must still be added by hand
Form submission behaviour like a real button
Nothing, roles are ignored on divs
check.why: ARIA changes what assistive tech announces, not behaviour. You still need tabindex, key handlers and disabled logic, which a native button gives you for free.

check.q: A page has three nav elements with no labels. What is the main problem for a screen-reader user?
options: The page fails HTML validation
Only the first nav is exposed
Search engines ignore the navigation
The landmarks list shows three identical 'navigation' entries they cannot tell apart
check.why: Multiple landmarks of the same type need distinct accessible names, for example aria-label="Primary" and aria-label="Footer".

check.q: A Cancel button inside a form submits the form when clicked. What is the most likely cause?
options: The button has no type attribute, and buttons in a form default to type="submit"
The form is missing novalidate
The button is not inside a fieldset
Cancel buttons must be links
check.why: A button element inside a form defaults to type="submit". Non-submit buttons need type="button".

lessons.title: The cascade, specificity, inheritance and the box model
lessons.summary: The exact order in which CSS decides a winning value, how layers and :where() change it, what inherits, and how boxes get their size.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Two mechanisms explain most "why does my CSS do that?" moments:
1. **The cascade** decides which declaration wins when several rules set the same property on the same element, and **inheritance** fills in properties nobody set.
2. **The box model and sizing** decide how big each box is once the winning values are known.

If you can reason about both from first principles, you stop fighting CSS with `!important` and magic numbers.

## How the cascade actually works
For every element and every property, the browser collects all matching declarations and sorts them by these criteria, in order. The first criterion that differs decides the winner:

```text
1. Origin and importance
     user-agent normal  <  user normal  <  author normal
     <  author !important  <  user !important  <  user-agent !important
     (animations and transitions slot in around these)
2. Context          (shadow DOM: outer page vs component styles)
3. Element-attached (the style="" attribute beats selectors)
4. Cascade layers   (@layer order)
5. Specificity      (inline-free selectors: ids, classes, types)
6. Order of appearance (last one wins)
```

Note that **layers come before specificity**. That is the whole point of `@layer`: a low-specificity selector in a later layer beats a high-specificity selector in an earlier layer.

### Specificity
Specificity is a three-part tuple compared left to right, never a base-10 number:
- **A**: id selectors (`#nav`)
- **B**: classes, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes (`.item`, `[type="text"]`, `:hover`)
- **C**: type selectors and pseudo-elements (`a`, `::before`)

`#nav .item a:hover` is (1, 2, 1). `.a.b.c.d.e.f.g.h.i.j.k` is (0, 11, 0) and still loses to a single id, because A is compared first.

The functional pseudo-classes are special:
- `:is()`, `:not()` and `:has()` take the specificity of their **most specific argument**. `:is(#hero, .card) p` is (1, 0, 1) even when it matches through `.card`.
- `:where()` always contributes **zero**. That makes it ideal for library defaults that should be trivially overridable.
- The universal selector `*` and combinators add nothing.

### Cascade layers
```css
/* Declare order once, up front. Later layers win. */
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  *, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
}

@layer components {
  #checkout .btn { background: var(--color-brand); } /* (1,1,0) */
}

@layer utilities {
  .bg-muted { background: var(--color-muted); }      /* (0,1,0) but wins */
}
```
Two rules surprise people:
- **Unlayered styles beat all layered styles** for normal declarations. Anything you write outside `@layer` acts like the last layer.
- **`!important` reverses layer order.** An `!important` in `reset` beats an `!important` in `utilities`. This lets a low layer protect something essential.

You can import third-party CSS straight into a layer: `@import url("vendor.css") layer(vendor);`. That is how you stop a component library from winning specificity wars against your code. Miriam Suzanne's complete guide to cascade layers on CSS-Tricks walks through these rules in detail.

## Inheritance and the global keywords
If no declaration wins for a property, the browser either **inherits** the parent's computed value (for inherited properties) or uses the **initial** value.
- Inherited: mostly text-related. `color`, `font-*`, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`, `text-align`, `visibility`, `cursor`, and **custom properties**.
- Not inherited: box-related. `margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`, `width`, `display`, `position`.

Every property accepts five global keywords:

| Keyword | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `inherit` | Take the parent's computed value, even for non-inherited properties |
| `initial` | The spec's initial value (`display: initial` is `inline`, not `block`) |
| `unset` | `inherit` if the property is inherited, otherwise `initial` |
| `revert` | Roll back to the previous origin (usually the browser default) |
| `revert-layer` | Roll back to the previous cascade layer |

`all: revert` on a component root is a handy way to undo page styles leaking in. `initial` is a common trap: `div { display: initial }` makes the div inline.

## The box model
```text
+----------------------------------------------+
|                    margin                    |
|   +--------------------------------------+   |
|   |               border                 |   |
|   |   +------------------------------+   |   |
|   |   |           padding            |   |   |
|   |   |   +----------------------+   |   |   |
|   |   |   |       content        |   |   |   |
|   |   |   +----------------------+   |   |   |
|   |   +------------------------------+   |   |
|   +--------------------------------------+   |
+----------------------------------------------+
```
With the default `box-sizing: content-box`, `width` sets only the content box, so `width: 100%; padding: 16px` overflows its parent by 32px plus borders. With `box-sizing: border-box`, `width` includes padding and border. Almost every reset sets `border-box` globally, as above.

### Margins behave differently from padding
- **Vertical margins between block siblings collapse**: 24px and 16px give a 24px gap, not 40px.
- A child's top margin can **escape through its parent** if the parent has no border, padding or new formatting context. Josh Comeau's "rules of margin collapse" covers every case.
- Margins never collapse in flex or grid containers. That is one reason `gap` is so pleasant: it only applies between items.
- Percentage padding and margin, even vertical ones, resolve against the containing block's **width**.

### Intrinsic and extrinsic sizing
- **Extrinsic**: the size comes from outside (`width: 300px`, `100%`, a grid track).
- **Intrinsic**: the size comes from content.
  - `min-content`: the narrowest the box can be without overflow (the longest word or widest image).
  - `max-content`: the width if text never wraps.
  - `fit-content`: `max-content`, but clamped to the available space. Great for a tag or a centred card that should hug its content.

```css
.tag { inline-size: fit-content; padding-inline: 0.5em; }
.layout { grid-template-columns: max-content 1fr; } /* label column hugs the longest label */
```

The `min-width: auto` default on flex and grid items resolves to the item's min-content size. That is why a long URL can blow out a flex layout; the fix (`min-width: 0`) is covered in the flexbox lesson.

### Display types
`display` has an **outer** type (how the box participates in its parent: `block` or `inline`) and an **inner** type (how its children are laid out: `flow`, `flex`, `grid`). `inline-flex` is "inline outside, flex inside". Inline boxes ignore `width`, `height` and vertical margins; `inline-block` respects them.

## Real example: overriding a library cleanly
Problem: a UI library ships `.lib-button.lib-button--primary { padding: 12px 24px }` and your utility `.p-2` will not override it.

```css
/* Old way: escalate */
.p-2 { padding: 8px !important; }

/* Better: put the library in a lower layer */
@layer vendor, app;
@import url("lib.css") layer(vendor);

@layer app {
  .p-2 { padding: 8px; } /* wins: app layer beats vendor layer */
}
```
No `!important`, no selector inflation, and the next developer can read the intended order at the top of the file. Note that `@import` must come before other rules, except `@layer` statements and `@charset`.

## Trade-offs and when not to use these tools
- **`!important`** is legitimate for utilities that must always win and for overriding inline styles you do not control. As a general fix it starts an arms race.
- **Ids in selectors** make overrides expensive. Use them for anchors and `aria-*` references, not styling.
- **Layers** add a concept the team must learn, and unlayered CSS silently beating everything surprises people. Adopt them with an agreed layer list in one file.
- **`:where()`** is ideal for library defaults, but zero specificity means *anything* overrides it, including rules you did not intend.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Treating specificity as base-10** ("11 classes beat 1 id"). They do not.
- **Expecting `width` to be inherited.** It is not; percentages resolve against the containing block instead.
- **Fighting with order of appearance across files.** Bundlers can reorder CSS chunks between routes. If correctness depends on file order, use layers or more explicit selectors.
- **Debugging:** in DevTools Elements, the Styles pane lists matching rules in cascade order with losers struck through, and the Computed pane shows the final value with a link to the winning rule. Hovering a selector shows its specificity in Chromium. The layer of each rule is shown too.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** the order of the cascade (especially that layers precede specificity), specificity as a tuple, how `:is()` and `:where()` change it, inheritance versus initial values, `box-sizing`, margin collapse.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. The cascade sorts declarations by origin and importance, then inline styles, then layers, then specificity, then source order.
2. Specificity is an (ids, classes, types) tuple compared left to right; `:where()` is zero and `:is()` takes its strongest argument.
3. Layers let you set precedence explicitly: later layers win regardless of specificity, unlayered beats layered, `!important` reverses it.
4. If nothing wins, inherited properties like `color` take the parent value; others take their initial value. `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert` and `revert-layer` control that by hand.
5. Then sizing: `border-box` makes width include padding and border; vertical margins collapse in normal flow but not in flex or grid.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "What is the specificity of this selector?", "Why does `display: initial` make a div inline?", "How would you stop a third-party stylesheet overriding yours?", "When do margins collapse?", "What is `fit-content` for?"
keyPoints: Cascade order: origin and importance, context, inline styles, layers, specificity, then source order. Layers come before specificity.
Specificity is an (ids, classes, types) tuple compared left to right; :is()/:not()/:has() take their strongest argument, :where() is zero.
Unlayered styles beat layered ones, and !important reverses layer order.
Text properties and custom properties inherit; box properties take their initial value. revert and revert-layer roll back to earlier origins or layers.
border-box makes width include padding and border; vertical margins collapse only in normal block flow.
interview: How do you calculate the specificity of a selector like #nav .item a:hover, and how do :is(), :where() and :not() change it?
Explain inheritance in CSS and the difference between inherit, initial, unset, revert and revert-layer.
What are the intrinsic sizing keywords min-content, max-content and fit-content, and when do they matter?

check.q: Rule A is `#app .card p` in @layer components. Rule B is `p` in @layer utilities, declared after components. Both set color. Which wins?
options: Rule A, because it has an id
Rule B, because layer order is compared before specificity
Whichever appears last in the file
Neither; the browser default is used
check.why: Cascade layers are sorted before specificity. A later layer wins regardless of selector specificity for normal declarations.

check.q: What is the specificity of `:where(#hero) .title::before`?
check.why: :where() contributes zero, .title adds one class and ::before is a pseudo-element counted with types, giving (0, 1, 1).

check.q: An element has width: 100%, padding: 20px and the default box-sizing. What happens?
options: It fits exactly inside its parent
The padding is ignored
It shrinks its content to fit
It overflows the parent by 40px plus any border
check.why: With content-box, width applies to the content only, so padding and border are added on top. border-box avoids this.

lessons.title: Flexbox and grid: how the algorithms size things
lessons.summary: Content-out flexbox versus layout-in grid, the flex shorthand, the min-width: auto trap, fr and minmax, auto-fit versus auto-fill, and accessible reordering.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Flexbox and grid are both layout algorithms you switch on with `display`. The useful distinction is not "1D versus 2D" alone, it is **who decides the sizes**:
- **Flexbox is content-out.** Items have a preferred size, and the algorithm distributes leftover space (or takes away overflow) along one axis. Each line is sized independently. Perfect for toolbars, nav bars, tag lists, and "push this to the end" alignments.
- **Grid is layout-in.** You define tracks (rows and columns) on the container, and items are placed into them. Rows and columns line up across the whole container. Perfect for page shells, card galleries, forms with aligned labels, and anything where things must line up in two directions.

Most real layouts use both: a grid for the page, flex inside the header.

## How flexbox sizes items
Each item has three numbers: `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink` and `flex-basis`.

```text
1. Determine each item's flex base size (flex-basis, or its content size if basis is auto).
2. Sum them, add gaps, compare with the container's main size.
3a. Free space > 0: share it in proportion to flex-grow.
3b. Free space < 0: take it away in proportion to flex-shrink x base size.
4. Clamp each item by min-width/max-width; if clamped, redistribute and repeat.
5. Wrap into lines if flex-wrap allows; align with justify-content (main axis)
   and align-items / align-self (cross axis).
```

The shorthands are where the bugs hide:

| Shorthand | Expands to | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `flex: initial` (default) | `0 1 auto` | Content-sized, may shrink, will not grow |
| `flex: auto` | `1 1 auto` | Starts from content size, shares leftover space |
| `flex: 1` | `1 1 0%` | Ignores content size, splits space equally |
| `flex: none` | `0 0 auto` | Rigid, content-sized |

So `flex: 1` on three items gives three **equal** columns (basis 0), while `flex: auto` gives columns that differ by content width. Josh Comeau's interactive guide to flexbox visualises this growing and shrinking very well.

### The min-width: auto trap
Flex items default to `min-width: auto`, which resolves to their **min-content** width. A long unbroken string (a URL, a code block, a wide table) therefore refuses to shrink and pushes the layout wider than the screen.

```css
.sidebar-layout { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
.sidebar-layout > main {
  flex: 1;
  min-width: 0;   /* allow shrinking below content; then overflow handles the rest */
}
.sidebar-layout pre { overflow-x: auto; }
```
The same thing happens in grid: `1fr` means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, so use `minmax(0, 1fr)` when a column must be allowed to shrink.

### Alignment you will use daily
```css
.toolbar { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem; }
.toolbar .spacer { margin-inline-start: auto; } /* pushes the rest to the end */

.center { display: grid; place-items: center; } /* the one-line centring */
```
Auto margins in flex absorb free space, which is cleaner than `justify-content: space-between` when only one item should move.

## How grid works
You define tracks; items flow into cells (auto-placement) or are placed explicitly.

```css
.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 16rem minmax(0, 1fr);
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "nav    main"
    "footer footer";
  min-block-size: 100dvh;
  gap: 1rem;
}
.page > header { grid-area: header; }
.page > nav    { grid-area: nav; }
.page > main   { grid-area: main; }
.page > footer { grid-area: footer; }

@media (width < 48rem) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr);
    grid-template-areas: "header" "main" "nav" "footer";
  }
}
```
Named areas make responsive rearrangement a one-line change. But note that **visual order is not DOM order**: keyboard focus and screen readers still follow the source. Reordering with areas, `order` or `grid-row` can create a confusing tab sequence; WCAG asks that meaningful sequence be preserved.

### Track sizing
- `fr` divides **leftover** space after fixed and content-sized tracks are resolved.
- `minmax(min, max)` sets a range.
- `auto` tracks size to content and then absorb leftover space when no `fr` tracks exist.
- `fit-content(20rem)` hugs content up to a cap.

### The responsive gallery without media queries
```css
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(15rem, 100%), 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}
```
Step by step: the browser fits as many 15rem-minimum columns as the width allows, then `1fr` stretches them to fill the row. `min(15rem, 100%)` stops a single column from overflowing on very narrow screens.

**`auto-fill` versus `auto-fit`:** both create as many tracks as fit. `auto-fill` keeps the empty tracks, so with two items on a wide screen they stay card-sized and leave space at the end. `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks to zero, so the two items stretch to fill the row. Use `auto-fill` when cards must keep a consistent width.

### Implicit grid and dense packing
Items beyond your defined rows create **implicit tracks** sized by `grid-auto-rows` (default `auto`). `grid-auto-flow: dense` backfills holes left by spanning items, which is nice for image mosaics but again breaks the link between visual and DOM order.

## A real example: a product card row that lines up
Cards in a row with a title, description and price: you want the prices aligned even when descriptions differ in length.

```css
.card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.5rem; }
.card .price { margin-block-start: auto; } /* stick to the bottom */
```
That aligns the *bottoms*. To align every internal row across cards (titles of different lengths too), use **subgrid** (see the modern CSS lesson), which lets each card adopt the parent grid's rows.

## Trade-offs and when not to use each
- **Flex for unknown, varying item counts** in one line (chips, buttons). Grid would force you to define tracks you do not know.
- **Grid when things must align in two directions** or when the container should own the layout. Flex-wrap rows never align columns between lines.
- **Do not use grid for every tiny row.** A button with an icon is `inline-flex` with `gap`.
- **Do not use floats for layout** in new code. They remain the right tool for wrapping text around an image (and `shape-outside`).
- **Tables are for tabular data.** `display: grid` on a `<table>` removes its semantics in some browsers; keep tables as tables and style them.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Overflow from long content** in flex or `1fr` tracks: add `min-width: 0` or use `minmax(0, 1fr)`.
- **`height: 100%` on a child of a flex item** that has no definite height. Let the flex item stretch (`align-items: stretch` is the default) instead, or make it a flex or grid container too.
- **Using margins on every item for spacing** and then fighting the last item. `gap` works in flex and grid in every current browser.
- **`justify-items` in flexbox**: it does nothing there. Flex uses `justify-content` and auto margins on the main axis.
- **Debugging:** DevTools in Chromium and Firefox have grid and flex overlays: click the `grid` or `flex` badge next to an element. They show track lines, area names, gaps and free space. Firefox's flexbox inspector even explains why an item grew or shrank.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** when you pick flex versus grid and why; whether you understand the flex shorthand; the min-width trap; `fr`, `minmax`, `auto-fit` versus `auto-fill`; and whether you mention source order and accessibility when reordering.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Flexbox distributes space along one axis based on item sizes (content-out). Grid defines tracks on the container and places items into them (layout-in), with rows and columns that line up.
2. `flex: 1` is `1 1 0%`, so items split space equally; `flex: auto` starts from content size.
3. Flex and grid items default to `min-width: auto`; long content overflows until you set `min-width: 0` or `minmax(0, 1fr)`.
4. `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(15rem, 1fr))` gives a responsive gallery without media queries; `auto-fill` keeps empty tracks, `auto-fit` collapses them.
5. Visual reordering does not change tab order or reading order, so reorder carefully.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "Build a holy-grail layout", "Why is my flex child overflowing?", "What does `fr` divide?", "How do you align items across cards?", "When would you still use a float?"
keyPoints: Flexbox distributes space along one axis from item sizes; grid defines tracks on the container so rows and columns align.
flex: 1 is 1 1 0% (equal shares); flex: auto is 1 1 auto (starts from content size).
Flex and grid items default to min-width: auto; fix overflow with min-width: 0 or minmax(0, 1fr).
repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(15rem, 100%), 1fr)) is a responsive gallery with no media queries; auto-fill keeps empty tracks.
Reordering with order, grid areas or dense packing does not change focus or reading order.
interview: What does flex: 1 actually mean, and why does a flex item sometimes refuse to shrink below its content?
How does repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) work, and how is auto-fit different from auto-fill?
How would you build a page shell with CSS grid, and how do grid-template-areas help with responsive layouts?

check.q: Three flex items have flex: 1 and very different text lengths. How wide are they?
options: Proportional to their text length
Equal widths, because flex: 1 sets flex-basis to 0%
As wide as their content, with leftover space at the end
The first item takes all the free space
check.why: flex: 1 expands to 1 1 0%. With a zero basis all space is free space, shared equally by grow factor (unless min-content forces an item wider).

check.q: A main column with flex: 1 contains a long URL and overflows the viewport. What is the usual fix?
options: Set flex-shrink: 10
Set width: 100% on the main column
Set min-width: 0 on the flex item (and handle overflow inside it)
Switch the container to display: block
check.why: Flex items default to min-width: auto, which resolves to min-content. min-width: 0 lets the item shrink below its content.

check.q: A gallery uses repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) and only has two items on a 1200px-wide screen. What do you see?
options: Two items stretched to 600px each
One item per row
The items overflow the container
Two roughly 200px-wide items with empty tracks after them
check.why: auto-fill keeps the empty tracks, so the items stay track-sized. auto-fit would collapse the empty tracks and stretch the two items.

lessons.title: Responsive design: viewport, fluid layout, images and queries
lessons.summary: The viewport meta tag, mobile-first rem breakpoints, media features, viewport units, fluid clamp() type that survives zoom, responsive images and container queries.
keyPoints: Without width=device-width the mobile layout viewport is about 980px wide and your media queries never fire; never block zoom.
Write mobile-first, put breakpoints in rem where content breaks, and lean on intrinsic layouts to need fewer of them.
clamp() fluid type must mix rem into the preferred value, or it stops responding to zoom and font settings.
srcset with sizes picks a resolution, picture handles art direction and formats; width and height attributes prevent layout shift.
Media queries for page layout and user preferences, container queries for reusable components.
interview: What does the viewport meta tag do, and why does a site look zoomed out on phones without it?
How do srcset, sizes and the picture element work for responsive images?
How do you build fluid typography with clamp() without breaking zoom accessibility?

check.q: An image uses srcset with width descriptors but no sizes attribute and renders as a 300px-wide thumbnail. What happens?
options: The browser ignores srcset
The browser assumes sizes is 100vw and may download a much larger file than needed
The browser always picks the smallest candidate
The image fails to render
check.why: sizes defaults to 100vw, so the browser picks a candidate for a full-viewport-width slot, wasting bytes on a thumbnail.

check.q: Why is `font-size: 4vw` a problem for accessibility?
options: vw is not supported on mobile
It breaks the cascade
It does not grow when the user zooms or raises their default font size
It causes layout shift on load
check.why: Viewport units track the viewport, not the user's font preferences. Mixing rem into the value (for example clamp(1rem, 0.9rem + 0.5vw, 1.25rem)) restores that.

check.q: A full-height mobile hero uses height: 100vh and its bottom is hidden behind the browser toolbar. Which unit fixes it most robustly?
options: 100svh (small viewport height)
100lvh (large viewport height)
100vmax
check.why: On mobile, vh equals the large viewport (toolbars retracted). svh is the small viewport, so the hero always fits; dvh tracks changes but can cause reflow.

lessons.title: Modern CSS: container queries, :has(), layers, nesting, subgrid, view transitions
lessons.summary: The features that changed CSS since 2022, the problem each solves and how it works: container queries, :has(), layers, nesting, subgrid, logical properties, view transitions.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Between 2022 and 2025 CSS gained more power than in the previous decade. Features that used to require JavaScript, preprocessors or awkward markup are now native and supported in every evergreen browser: **container queries**, **`:has()`**, **cascade layers**, **nesting**, **subgrid**, **logical properties** and **view transitions** (same-document first, cross-document arriving). Interviewers ask about them to see whether your CSS knowledge is current and whether you understand the *problem* each one solves, not just the syntax.

A useful filter for "can I use it?" is **Baseline** (shown on MDN and web.dev): "Newly available" means it works in the latest Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari; "Widely available" means it has done so for 30 months. Everything in this lesson except cross-document view transitions is at least newly available.

## Container queries
**Problem:** a component's layout should depend on the space *it* gets, not the viewport. The same card sits in a sidebar and a main column.

```css
.product-slot { container: product / inline-size; }

.product { display: grid; gap: 0.75rem; }

@container product (inline-size >= 28rem) {
  .product { grid-template-columns: 8rem 1fr; align-items: start; }
}
@container product (inline-size >= 48rem) {
  .product { grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr auto; }
}

.product__title { font-size: clamp(1rem, 3cqi + 0.5rem, 1.5rem); }
```
How it works: `container-type: inline-size` applies **size containment** on the inline axis, meaning the element's width no longer depends on its contents. That breaks the circularity ("my width depends on my child, my child's style depends on my width") that made container queries impossible for years. Consequences:
- An element cannot query itself, only an ancestor container.
- A container with `inline-size` containment that is shrink-wrapped (say, a float or inline-block with no width) collapses to zero width. Containers should be block-level or have a definite width.
- Units `cqi`, `cqb`, `cqw`, `cqh`, `cqmin`, `cqmax` are percentages of the nearest container.
- **Style queries** (`@container style(--variant: compact)`) query custom property values. Support has lagged size queries, so check before relying on them.

## :has(), the parent selector and more
`:has()` matches an element if the relative selector inside matches something relative to it. It is the long-requested parent selector, and much more:

```css
/* A card with an image gets a two-column layout */
.card:has(> img) { grid-template-columns: 8rem 1fr; }

/* Style a field wrapper when its input is invalid after interaction */
.field:has(input:user-invalid) { --border-color: var(--color-danger); }

/* Previous-sibling: the label before a focused input */
label:has(+ input:focus-visible) { color: var(--color-brand); }

/* Page-level state without JS: lock scroll while a modal dialog is open */
html:has(dialog[open]:modal) { overflow: hidden; }

/* Quantity query: a grid with 5 or more items */
.grid:has(> :nth-child(5)) { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
```
Gotchas: specificity is that of its most specific argument; `:has()` cannot be nested inside another `:has()`; and pseudo-elements are not allowed inside it. Performance is good in practice, but very broad anchors like `body:has(.x)` re-evaluate on many DOM changes, so scope them where you can.

## Cascade layers
`@layer reset, base, components, utilities;` declares precedence once. Later layers beat earlier ones **before specificity is considered**; unlayered styles beat all layers; `!important` reverses the order. The killer use case is taming third-party CSS: `@import url("lib.css") layer(vendor);`. Tailwind CSS v4 itself emits its output into layers (`theme`, `base`, `components`, `utilities`). See the cascade lesson for the full rules.

## Native nesting
```css
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--border);

  & h3 { margin-block: 0 0.5rem; }      /* .card h3 */
  &:hover { border-color: var(--brand); } /* .card:hover */
  .theme-dark & { background: var(--surface-dark); } /* .theme-dark .card */

  @media (width >= 48rem) {             /* nested at-rules work too */
    padding: 1.5rem;
  }
}
```
Differences from Sass, the classic interview probe:
- **No string concatenation.** `&__title` (the BEM trick) does not work natively; `&` is a selector, not text.
- **`&` behaves like `:is()`.** `.a, #b { & .c {} }` becomes `:is(.a, #b) .c`, whose specificity is that of `#b` even when matching via `.a`. Sass would produce two separate selectors.
- Early implementations required a selector to start with a symbol (so `& h3`, not `h3`). Current browsers accept bare element selectors (the "relaxed" syntax); writing `&` explicitly is still clearer.
- It runs in the browser, so no build step. You may still want a preprocessor or Lightning CSS for older-browser output.

Deep nesting is still a smell: it inflates specificity and couples CSS to DOM structure. Keep it to one or two levels.

## Subgrid
**Problem:** in a row of cards, each card is its own layout, so titles of different lengths push descriptions and buttons out of alignment between cards.

```css
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(16rem, 1fr));
  gap: 1.5rem;
}
.card {
  display: grid;
  grid-row: span 3;             /* occupy 3 rows of the parent */
  grid-template-rows: subgrid;  /* and adopt those row tracks */
  gap: 0.5rem;                  /* can override the parent's gap */
}
```
```text
Without subgrid               With subgrid
+--------+ +--------+         +--------+ +--------+
| Title  | | Long   |         | Title  | | Long   |
| desc   | | title  |         |        | | title  |
| [Buy]  | | desc   |         | desc   | | desc   |
+--------+ | [Buy]  |         | [Buy]  | | [Buy]  |
           +--------+         +--------+ +--------+
```
Every card's title row is now the same track, sized by the tallest title. Subgrid also passes line names down, and works for columns: a form where nested fieldsets keep labels aligned with the outer label column.

## Logical properties
Physical properties (`margin-left`, `width`, `top`) assume left-to-right, horizontal text. Logical properties follow the **writing mode and direction**:

| Physical | Logical |
|---|---|
| `width` / `height` | `inline-size` / `block-size` |
| `margin-left` / `margin-right` | `margin-inline-start` / `margin-inline-end` |
| `padding-top` + `padding-bottom` | `padding-block` |
| `top` / `left` | `inset-block-start` / `inset-inline-start` |
| `text-align: left` | `text-align: start` |

Set `dir="rtl"` on Arabic or Hebrew pages and a layout written with logical properties mirrors correctly with no extra CSS. Vertical writing modes (`writing-mode: vertical-rl`, used in Japanese and for rotated labels) also just work. Shorthands like `margin-inline: auto` are terser even for LTR-only sites.

## View transitions
**Problem:** animating between two UI states (a list item expanding into a detail page) used to mean keeping both states in the DOM and hand-writing FLIP animations.

**Same-document** (SPAs):
```js
function navigate(update) {
  if (!document.startViewTransition) return update();   // progressive enhancement
  document.startViewTransition(() => update());           // update can return a promise
}
```
```css
.thumb  { view-transition-name: hero-image; }  /* on the list page */
.detail-hero { view-transition-name: hero-image; } /* on the detail view */

::view-transition-old(root),
::view-transition-new(root) { animation-duration: 200ms; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-group(*) { animation: none; }
}
```
How it works, step by step:
```text
1. startViewTransition(cb): browser snapshots the current state (old images)
2. Rendering is paused; cb runs and updates the DOM
3. Browser snapshots the new state (live new images)
4. It builds a pseudo-element tree in the top layer:
     ::view-transition
       ::view-transition-group(hero-image)
         ::view-transition-image-pair(hero-image)
           ::view-transition-old(hero-image)   (screenshot)
           ::view-transition-new(hero-image)   (live)
5. Default: groups animate size/position; old fades out, new fades in
6. Animations finish, the pseudo tree is removed
```
Each `view-transition-name` must be **unique** on the page at the moment of capture, otherwise the transition is skipped. The old state is a static image, so animated content inside it freezes for the duration.

**Cross-document** (MPAs): opt in on both pages with `@view-transition { navigation: auto; }`, same-origin only. Chromium and Safari support it; check current Firefox support before relying on it, and treat it as an enhancement. Same-document transitions are supported in Chromium, Safari 18+ and recent Firefox. React and Next.js have been adding integrations, so check your framework's docs.

## Trade-offs and when not to use them
- **Container queries** add containment: the container cannot size to its content on that axis. Do not make every div a container; wrap component slots.
- **`:has()`** can replace a lot of JavaScript state classes, but logic hidden in selectors is harder to trace than an explicit `data-state` attribute. Use it for presentational relationships.
- **Nesting** encourages over-specific selectors. Flat class-based CSS is still easier to override.
- **View transitions** are visual polish; they block interaction during the animation, and long or frequent transitions annoy users. Keep them short and respect reduced motion.
- **Logical properties** have almost no downside, but mixing physical and logical properties for the same side creates confusion; pick one convention.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Querying a container that has no `container-type`: the query silently never matches. DevTools shows a `container` badge on containers.
- Expecting `&__elem` to work in native nesting.
- Duplicate `view-transition-name`s, which abort the transition with a console warning. Assign names dynamically only to the element being transitioned.
- Using `:has()` inside `:has()`; it is invalid, and an invalid selector drops the whole rule (a forgiving selector list inside `:is()` or `:where()` avoids that for other cases).
- **Debugging view transitions:** the Animations panel in Chromium DevTools can pause and scrub them, and the pseudo-elements appear in the Elements panel during the transition.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you know what each feature replaces, how containment makes container queries possible, `:has()` beyond "parent selector", nesting versus Sass, why subgrid exists, and how view transitions work and degrade.

**A 60-second answer outline:**
1. Container queries let components respond to their container's size; they rely on size containment, which is why an element cannot query itself.
2. `:has()` styles an element based on its descendants or following siblings: parent, previous-sibling and page-state selectors without JavaScript.
3. Layers make precedence explicit; nesting removes a reason for Sass but has no string concatenation and wraps the parent in `:is()`.
4. Subgrid lets nested elements share the parent's tracks, so content aligns across cards or form sections.
5. Logical properties make layouts work in RTL and vertical writing modes; view transitions snapshot old and new states and animate between them, with a fallback when unsupported.

**Follow-ups to expect:** "How does native nesting differ from Sass?", "Give a real subgrid example", "How do view transitions work and what are their limits?", "Why would you use `margin-inline-start`?", "When would `:has()` be the wrong tool?"
keyPoints: Container queries rely on size containment, so an element can only query an ancestor container, never itself.
:has() gives parent, previous-sibling and page-state selectors; it takes its strongest argument's specificity and cannot nest.
Native nesting has no string concatenation (&__elem fails) and wraps the parent list in :is(), unlike Sass.
Subgrid lets children adopt the parent's tracks, so titles, text and buttons align across a row of cards.
Logical properties follow writing mode and direction; view transitions snapshot old and new states and animate pseudo-elements, with a fallback when unsupported.
interview: How does native CSS nesting work, and how is it different from Sass nesting?
What problem does CSS subgrid solve? Give a real example.
How does the View Transitions API work, and what are its limits?
What are CSS logical properties, and why would you use margin-inline-start instead of margin-left?

check.q: Why can an element not respond to its own size with a container query?
options: Browsers have not implemented it yet
Containers apply size containment, and styling an element by its own size would be circular
Container queries only work on the body element
It is possible with container-type: self
check.why: Containment makes the container's size independent of its contents so descendants can be styled by it. Querying itself would reintroduce the circular dependency.

check.q: In native CSS nesting, what does `.btn { &--primary { color: red } }` do?
options: Generates .btn--primary like Sass
Generates .btn .--primary
It does not produce .btn--primary; & is a selector, not text to concatenate
Throws a JavaScript error
check.why: Native nesting treats & as a selector reference, so BEM-style suffix concatenation from Sass does not work.

check.q: A view transition is skipped with a console warning. Two list items both have view-transition-name: card. What is wrong?
options: Names must be unique among rendered elements at capture time
Names must start with a double dash
view-transition-name only works on images
Transitions require a cross-document opt-in
check.why: Each view-transition-name must be unique when the old and new states are captured; duplicates abort the transition.

lessons.title: CSS architecture: BEM, CSS Modules, Tailwind, CSS-in-JS and design tokens
lessons.summary: How teams keep CSS scoped and consistent at scale, the real trade-offs between BEM, CSS Modules, utility-first and CSS-in-JS, and how to build tokens and themes.
lessons.body:
## The core idea CSS has one global namespace and a cascade where any rule can affect any element. That is fine for a page and painful for a product with 50 engineers. **CSS architecture** is the set of conventions and tools that keep styles **scoped** (a change here does not break something there), **predictable** (you can tell what wins), **deletable** (you know when a rule is unused) and **consistent** (everyone uses the same colours and spacing). Every approach answers the same four questions differently: 1. How are styles scoped to a component? 2. Where do styles live relative to markup? 3. When is CSS generated: at build time or at runtime? 4. How are design decisions (colours, spacing, type) shared? ## The main approaches ```text scoping when generated where it lives BEM / plain CSS naming rules author time .css files CSS Modules hashed classes build time .module.css next to component Utility-first no scoping need build time class names in markup (Tailwind) (atomic) Runtime CSS-in-JS generated class runtime (JS) JS/TS in component (styled-components, Emotion) Zero-runtime generated class build time TS in component CSS-in-JS (vanilla-extract, Panda CSS, StyleX, Linaria) ``` ### BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) ```css .card {} .card__title {} .card__title--featured {} .card--compact {} ``` A naming convention, not a tool. Every selector is one class, so specificity stays flat at (0,1,0) and order is predictable. Pros: zero tooling, works everywhere, readable in DevTools. Cons: it is only a convention, so nothing enforces it; names get long; dead CSS is hard to find because nothing links a class to its usage. ### CSS Modules ```css /* card.module.css */ .root { padding: var(--space-4); } .title { font: var(--font-heading); } ``` ```tsx import styles from "./card.module.css"; export function Card({ title }: { title: string }) { return

{title}

; } ``` The build rewrites `.root` to something like `.card_root__x7f2a`, so class names cannot collide. You write real CSS with all its features (container queries, `:has()`, nesting) and it is extracted to static files, with no runtime cost. Supported out of the box by Next.js and Vite. Cons: styling based on props needs class toggling or data attributes; sharing values with TypeScript requires custom properties or a separate tokens file; unused classes are not flagged unless you add a lint rule. ### Utility-first (Tailwind CSS) ```tsx ``` Each class does one thing. The tool scans your source files and generates only the classes you use. Pros: CSS size stops growing with features (a new page mostly reuses existing utilities); no naming; constraints come from the theme (you pick `px-4`, not `17px`); styles are deleted with the markup; very fast iteration. Cons: long class strings (mitigated with components and helpers like `cva` and `tailwind-merge`); the team must learn the vocabulary; complex selectors and animations are awkward inline; dynamic class names built from strings (`bg-${color}-500`) are invisible to the scanner and silently missing. Tailwind v4 (2025) moved configuration into CSS (`@theme { --color-brand: ... }`), exposes theme values as CSS custom properties, and emits output in cascade layers. That makes it interoperate better with plain CSS. ### Runtime CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion) ```tsx const Button = styled.button<{ $variant: "primary" | "ghost" }>` padding: 8px 16px; background: ${(p) => (p.$variant === "primary" ? p.theme.brand : "transparent")}; `; ``` Styles are written in JavaScript, serialised and injected into a style element at runtime. Pros: colocation, full JS power for dynamic styles, theming via context, scoped by default. Cons, and why the industry moved away: - **Runtime cost**: serialising styles and inserting rules during render adds work to every render, especially for components whose props change often. Sam Magura, an Emotion maintainer, wrote "Why we're breaking up with CSS-in-JS" after measuring this in a real app. - **React Server Components**: these libraries rely on React context and client-side rendering hooks, so styled components have to be client components. With streaming SSR they also need special integration to collect and inject styles in the right order. - **Bundle size**: the library ships to the client. - styled-components announced it was entering maintenance mode in 2025, which pushed many teams to migrate. ### Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS vanilla-extract, Panda CSS, Linaria and Meta's StyleX keep the authoring experience (type-safe styles in TypeScript, colocated) but extract static CSS at build time. StyleX compiles to atomic classes, similar in output to Tailwind. You give up runtime-computed values; dynamic values flow through CSS custom properties instead. ## Design tokens: the layer under all of them **Design tokens** are named design decisions: `color.brand.500`, `space.4`, `radius.md`, `font.body`. They are stored platform-neutrally (often JSON in the W3C Design Tokens Community Group format) and transformed into CSS custom properties, Tailwind theme values, iOS and Android constants. A tool like Style Dictionary does the transformation. Use two or three tiers: ```css :root { /* primitive: the palette */ --blue-600: oklch(0.55 0.2 260); --gray-50: oklch(0.98 0 0); --gray-900: oklch(0.2 0 0); /* semantic: what it is for (components only use these) */ --color-bg: var(--gray-50); --color-fg: var(--gray-900); --color-primary: var(--blue-600); --space-4: 1rem; --radius-md: 0.5rem; } [data-theme="dark"] { --color-bg: var(--gray-900); --color-fg: var(--gray-50); color-scheme: dark; } .button { background: var(--color-primary); border-radius: var(--radius-md); } ``` Components reference **semantic** tokens, so dark mode, high contrast or a white-label theme is just a different set of semantic values. Because custom properties inherit and resolve at runtime, theme switching costs one attribute change, with no re-render and no new CSS. Avoid a flash of the wrong theme by setting the attribute before first paint (an inline snippet in the head that reads the saved preference, or server-rendering it from a cookie). `@property` lets you register a custom property with a type (`syntax: ""`), which makes it animatable and type-checked; plain custom properties are untyped strings until used. ## How to choose (a defensible 2026 answer) For a large React or Next.js app using Server Components: - **Tailwind (or another build-time atomic system) plus a small component library** built on tokens, when the team values speed and consistency. This is the most common choice in new projects, and it is what shadcn/ui-style component kits assume. - **CSS Modules plus custom-property tokens** when the team prefers writing real CSS, or the design has many complex selectors and animations. - **Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS** when type-safe style APIs matter (a design system consumed by many teams). - **Avoid introducing runtime CSS-in-JS** in new RSC apps. For an existing styled-components codebase, migrate gradually, component by component, rather than in a big bang. Whatever you pick: tokens as the source of truth, one approach per codebase (mixing three systems is the real failure mode), cascade layers to order resets, vendor and utilities, and lint rules (Stylelint, a Tailwind class-order plugin). ## Common mistakes and debugging - **Specificity creep**: nested selectors in BEM or Sass (`.page .sidebar .card__title`) defeat the flat specificity BEM promises. - **Dynamic Tailwind classes** built from template strings: write full class names in a lookup object instead. - **Overriding component styles with `!important`** because the component did not expose a variant or a `className` prop. Design the API (variants, slots) instead. - **Hard-coded values** (`#3b82f6`, `13px`) that bypass tokens. Lint for raw colours. - **Theme flash** on load from applying the theme in a `useEffect`. - **Measuring the cost:** the Chrome Performance panel shows "Recalculate style" time; a React Profiler flame chart reveals CSS-in-JS work during render; the Coverage tab shows unused CSS bytes. ## In the interview **What they probe:** whether you can compare approaches on scoping, runtime cost, RSC compatibility, maintainability and team fit, rather than declaring a favourite; whether you know why runtime CSS-in-JS lost ground; and whether you can design a token and theming system. **A 60-second answer outline:** 1. The problem is global scope and the cascade at team scale; every approach trades off scoping, when CSS is generated, and colocation. 2. BEM is a naming convention with flat specificity; CSS Modules hash class names at build time; Tailwind generates only used atomic utilities; runtime CSS-in-JS injects styles during render. 3. Runtime CSS-in-JS costs render time and does not fit Server Components and streaming well, so new apps choose build-time options. 4. Tokens underneath: primitive and semantic custom properties, themes as attribute-scoped overrides, no flash on load. 5. My default for a large RSC app: Tailwind or CSS Modules on top of tokens, one approach per codebase, enforced by lint rules. **Follow-ups to expect:** "How would you migrate off styled-components?", "How do you implement dark mode without a flash?", "What goes in a semantic versus a primitive token?", "How do you stop Tailwind class strings becoming unreadable?", "Where do cascade layers fit?"
keyPoints: Every approach answers: how styles are scoped, where they live, when CSS is generated and how design decisions are shared.
CSS Modules and Tailwind generate static CSS at build time; runtime CSS-in-JS serialises and injects styles during render.
Runtime CSS-in-JS lost ground because of render cost, client bundle size and poor fit with Server Components and streaming.
Design tokens in tiers: primitives for the palette, semantic tokens for components; themes swap semantic values via custom properties.
Pick one approach per codebase and enforce it with lint rules; mixing systems is the usual failure.
interview: Compare BEM, CSS Modules, Tailwind and CSS-in-JS. Which would you pick for a large React app and why?
Why has runtime CSS-in-JS fallen out of favour with React Server Components and streaming?
What are design tokens, and how would you implement theming, including dark mode, with them?

check.q: A Tailwind project builds class names like `bg-${color}-500` from props. Some colours never appear. Why?
options: Tailwind does not support dynamic colours
The classes are purged by the browser
The scanner only finds complete class names in source, so these classes are never generated
Template strings break JSX
check.why: Tailwind generates CSS for class names it can see in your files. Build the full names in a lookup object so the scanner finds them.

check.q: What is the main reason to have components reference semantic tokens like --color-primary rather than primitives like --blue-600?
options: Themes can remap semantic tokens without touching component CSS
Semantic tokens render faster
Primitives are not valid custom property names
Browsers cannot inherit primitive tokens
check.why: Dark mode, high contrast or a white-label brand becomes a different set of semantic values; components stay unchanged.

check.q: How do CSS Modules prevent class name collisions?
options: By injecting styles at runtime with unique ids
By wrapping each component in shadow DOM
By forbidding global selectors in the browser
By rewriting class names to unique hashed names at build time
check.why: The bundler rewrites .title to something like .card_title__x7f2a and exports the mapping, so names are local to the file.

lessons.title: Animations: transitions, keyframes, the compositor, FLIP and reduced motion
lessons.summary: Why transform and opacity animate smoothly, when to use transitions, keyframes or the Web Animations API, how FLIP animates layout, and how to respect reduced motion.
keyPoints: Animating transform and opacity can skip layout and paint and run on the compositor; width, top and margin force layout every frame.
Transitions animate between two states on a change; keyframes handle loops and steps; WAAPI adds runtime keyframes and playback control.
FLIP measures First and Last, Inverts with a transform and Plays it back, so layout runs once instead of every frame.
Use will-change sparingly, list explicit transition properties and keep durations around 100 to 400ms.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion by reducing motion (fades instead of slides), not only removing it.
interview: CSS transitions, keyframe animations or the Web Animations API: when would you use each?

check.q: Which animation is most likely to stay smooth while the main thread is busy running JavaScript?
options: Animating left from 0 to 200px
Animating width from 0 to 100%
Animating transform: translateX() on an element with its own layer
Animating box-shadow
check.why: Transform and opacity animations can run on the compositor thread without layout or paint, so main-thread work does not stall them.

check.q: In FLIP, what does the Invert step do?
options: Reverses the DOM order
Applies a transform that makes the element appear at its old position after the layout change
Swaps the start and end keyframes
Inverts the colours for contrast
check.why: After measuring first and last positions, you apply a transform that visually puts the element back at First, then animate that transform to none.

check.q: A user has Reduce motion enabled. What is the best handling of a page that slides panels in?
options: Replace the slide with a short cross-fade and keep the state change visible
Ignore it; motion is part of the brand
Slow the slide down to be gentler
Disable the panels entirely
check.why: Reduce, do not remove: large movement is the trigger, so swap it for a subtle opacity change while keeping the feedback.

lessons.title: Forms: labels, input types, native validation and styling controls
lessons.summary: Accessible labels and groups, input types and autocomplete for mobile, the constraint validation API with custom error UI, :user-invalid, and styling native controls safely.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Forms are where users give you money, data and patience, and where most accessibility bugs live. The platform does a lot for you if you let it: **labels** that name fields and enlarge click targets, **input types** that pick the right mobile keyboard, **autocomplete** that fills a checkout in one tap, and **constraint validation** that blocks bad submissions without a line of JavaScript. Good form engineering means using those features first, then layering custom behaviour where the native version falls short, without losing what you started with. ## Labels: every control needs a name ```html

At least 12 characters.

``` A `
keyPoints: Every control needs a visible, associated label; placeholders vanish while typing and are not a reliable name.
Input types, inputmode and autocomplete tokens give the right keyboard and one-tap filling; avoid type=number for identifiers.
For custom error UI keep the engine: novalidate plus checkValidity, ValidityState, aria-invalid, aria-describedby and focus on the first error.
:user-invalid only matches after interaction, unlike :invalid, which marks empty required fields red on load.
Style the real input with accent-color or appearance: none, test forced-colors mode, and always revalidate on the server.
interview: How does native HTML form validation work, and when would you replace it with custom validation?
How do you label form inputs accessibly, and why is a placeholder not a label?
Which input types and attributes improve form UX on mobile?
How do you style checkboxes, selects and other native form controls without losing accessibility?

check.q: A form uses novalidate. What still works?
options: The browser's error bubbles on submit
Nothing; validation attributes are ignored completely
The validity API (checkValidity, ValidityState) based on required, pattern and other attributes
Only server-side validation
check.why: novalidate only stops the browser blocking submit and showing its own messages. Constraints are still evaluated, so you can render your own UI from them.

check.q: Why is input:user-invalid usually better than input:invalid for red error borders?
options: It is faster to match
It only matches after the user has interacted with the field or tried to submit
It works without the required attribute
It also checks server-side errors
check.why: :invalid matches immediately, so empty required fields are red on page load. :user-invalid waits for interaction.

check.q: What is the best markup for a 6-digit SMS verification code field?
options: type="number" maxlength="6"
type="password"
type="tel" with no autocomplete
type="text" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code"
check.why: This gives a digit keypad, lets the OS suggest the code from the SMS, and avoids number-input problems such as spinners and stripped leading zeros.

projects.title: Responsive, accessible marketing site with modern CSS
stack: Astro (static output) or Next.js static export
projects.summary: A multi-page product marketing site built with semantic HTML and modern CSS: token-driven themes with dark mode, container-query components, a responsive image pipeline, accessible motion and a validated contact form, gated by accessibility and performance checks in CI.
projects.why: Marketing sites are where frontend craft is most visible: every hiring manager can open it on their phone. This project proves you can ship pixel-solid, fast, accessible pages without hiding behind a component library, and that you know current CSS (container queries, :has(), layers, subgrid, view transitions) and can defend the trade-offs. The CI gates turn 'I care about accessibility and Core Web Vitals' into numbers you can show.
projects.architecture:
```text
content (Markdown/JSON)      tokens.json (DTCG)        images (originals)
        |                          |                         |
        v                          v                         v
  static site build  <-----  Style Dictionary  ----->  image step (AVIF/WebP/JPEG,
  (Astro or Next export)     -> tokens.css               widths 480..1920, dims)
        |
        v
  HTML pages: semantic landmarks, picture + srcset/sizes, contact form
  CSS: @layer reset, tokens, base, layout, components, utilities
       page grid = media queries | components = container queries
  JS (tiny): theme bootstrap, FLIP reorder, view transitions, form errors
        |
        v
  CI: Playwright (3 viewports, reduced motion, rtl) + axe-core + Lighthouse CI budgets
        |
        v
  static hosting + CDN; contact form -> serverless function (zod revalidation)
```
Key decisions: no UI framework or component library, so the CSS skills are visible; semantic tokens as the only colour source, themed with a data attribute set before first paint; cascade layers instead of specificity wars; container queries for components and media queries only for the page shell; static output for a fast LCP; JavaScript limited to progressive enhancements, so the site works with scripts disabled; accessibility and performance enforced as CI budgets rather than good intentions.

deepDives.title: Token pipeline and theming without a flash
Container queries versus media queries in this site
Image pipeline and LCP
deepDives.body:
The hero image is the LCP element on most pages, so it gets special treatment.

**Generation:** a build step (Astro's image service, or sharp in a script) produces each source at widths such as 480, 960, 1440 and 1920 in AVIF and WebP, plus a JPEG fallback. Each output records its intrinsic width and height.

**Markup:** a picture element with type-specific sources lists the candidates with width descriptors. The `sizes` attribute describes the rendered slot, for example `(width >= 64rem) 50vw, 100vw` for a split hero. Getting `sizes` wrong is the most common waste: without it the browser assumes 100vw and a 300px thumbnail downloads a 1920px file. The width and height attributes let the browser reserve the aspect ratio before the bytes arrive, which keeps CLS near zero.

**Priority:** the hero gets `fetchpriority="high"` and is never lazy-loaded; everything below the fold uses `loading="lazy"` and `decoding="async"`. Fonts are subset, self-hosted, preloaded for the one weight used above the fold, with `font-display: swap` and fallback metric overrides (`size-adjust`) to limit layout shift when they swap.

**Measuring:** Lighthouse CI runs on a throttled mobile profile and fails the PR if LCP exceeds the budget. The talking point is the before and after: bytes per device class and LCP from the lab, then confirmed with field data if the site has real traffic.

deepDives.title: Motion system and reduced motion
deepDives.body:
Motion is defined as tokens: `--duration-fast: 120ms`, `--duration-base: 200ms`, `--duration-slow: 320ms`, and two easings (`--ease-out`, `--ease-in-out`). Components only transition `transform`, `opacity` and colours, so animations stay on the compositor and never trigger layout.

**Testimonials reorder** uses FLIP: measure every card's rect, reorder the DOM, measure again, apply inverse transforms, and animate them to none with the Web Animations API. Reads are batched before writes to avoid layout thrashing.

**Blog navigation** uses same-document view transitions where `document.startViewTransition` exists; the post thumbnail and the post hero share a `view-transition-name` that is assigned only to the clicked item, because duplicate names abort the transition. Unsupported browsers simply navigate.

**Reduced motion:** all movement lives inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`, so the default is still. With Reduce motion on, slides become short opacity fades, FLIP is skipped (items just appear in place), view transitions fall back to a cross-fade or none, and nothing auto-plays. The JavaScript checks `matchMedia` and listens for changes. A Playwright test launches with `reducedMotion: 'reduce'` and asserts that no animated element has a non-identity transform mid-animation.

deepDives.title: Cascade layers as the stylesheet architecture
deepDives.body:
The entire stylesheet declares its order in one line at the top:

```css
@layer reset, tokens, base, layout, components, utilities;
```

- **reset**: box-sizing, margin resets, media defaults.
- **tokens**: custom properties only.
- **base**: element styles (body text, headings, links, focus-visible ring).
- **layout**: page grid, stack and cluster primitives.
- **components**: cards, nav, pricing, form controls, each in its own file.
- **utilities**: a handful of single-purpose classes (visually-hidden, flow spacing) that must always win.

Because layer order beats specificity, a utility with one class reliably overrides a component selector, and nobody writes `!important`. Third-party CSS (a syntax highlighter theme for the blog) is imported into its own early layer with `@import url(...) layer(vendor)`, so it can never override our components.

Two rules the team had to learn: unlayered CSS beats every layer (so all project CSS must be inside a layer, enforced by a lint check), and `!important` reverses layer order (so the reset can protect essentials like `[hidden] { display: none !important }`). DevTools shows each rule's layer, which makes debugging precedence straightforward.
